summary: This RFC explains how Label Switched Path (LSP) attributes are carried in RSVP-TE Path and Resv messages for MPLS. It specifies the message formats using Routing Backus-Naur Form and clarifies earlier text about handling these attribute objects.

eli5.summary: Roads in a network can have special rules, such as who may use them. This describes where in the setup messages those rules are written, and in what format.

questions: how are lsp attributes carried in rsvp
rsvp path and resv message formats
what is the lsp attributes object
how does rsvp-te report p2mp lsp status
subtitle: The exact message layouts for carrying LSP attributes in RSVP-TE Path and Resv messages, including per-leaf status for multicast LSPs.

tldr.problem: RFC 5420 defined LSP Attributes objects but only described their message placement in prose, which left open how to handle them in Resv messages of point-to-multipoint LSPs.
tldr.mechanism: This document gives the Routing Backus-Naur Form for Path and Resv messages carrying the objects, and lets each S2L sub-LSP report its own operational status by following its S2L_SUB_LSP object.
tldr.outcome: The objects are carried clearly for all LSP types, and different egress routers can report different statuses. It updates RFC 4875 and RFC 5420.

today: RFC 6510 is a Proposed Standard from February 2012 that updates RFC 4875 and RFC 5420. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: The Gap in LSP Attribute Signaling
sections.content:
Signaling for point-to-point MPLS and GMPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs) is defined in RFC 3209 and RFC 3473. RFC 4875 adds point-to-multipoint (P2MP) Traffic Engineering LSPs.

RFC 5420 defines two LSP Attributes objects. In a Path message they say how an LSP should be set up. In a Resv message they say how it has been established. RFC 5420 described the message formats only in narrative text, without the Routing Backus-Naur Form (RFC 5511) normally used for RSVP messages. That left open how to process the objects in Resv messages of P2MP LSPs.

This document supplies the BNF for Path and Resv messages carrying the object and clarifies how it is carried for all LSP types. Unmodified formats are not listed.
sections.eli5: The old rules explained where to put special notes in words only. This RFC draws the exact form, because nobody was sure what to do on roads that branch.

sections.title: Path Message Format
sections.content:
Path message formatting is unmodified from RFC 5420's narrative. The LSP_ATTRIBUTES and LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES objects MAY be carried in a Path message. They are RECOMMENDED to sit immediately after SESSION_ATTRIBUTE if present, or otherwise after LABEL_REQUEST. If both are present, LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES goes first.

Object order is only recommended: LSRs MUST accept these objects in any order and position. Later instances within a Path message SHOULD be ignored and MUST be forwarded unchanged.

The Path BNF places [ <LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES> ... ] and [ <LSP_ATTRIBUTES> ... ] after the optional SESSION_ATTRIBUTE. PathErr and PathTear messages are not affected.
sections.eli5: The special-rules notes go right after the label that names the road. They are not strict about order, and a second copy of the same note is ignored but passed along.

sections.title: Resv Messages and Per-LSP Status
sections.content:
In a Resv message, LSP_ATTRIBUTES MAY be carried. It sits in the flow descriptor, is associated with the preceding FILTER_SPEC, and is RECOMMENDED to follow the LABEL object. Only one instance per FILTER_SPEC is meaningful; extras SHOULD be ignored and MUST be forwarded unchanged.

This gives attributes per sender (LSP) and allows modification using make-before-break. That is enough for point-to-point LSPs and for the special case where all P2MP source-to-leaf (S2L) sub-LSPs report the same operational status. It does not let different egress LSRs report different statuses.

Section 3.1 gives the Resv BNF for per-LSP status, with LSP_ATTRIBUTES after LABEL in the FF flow descriptor and the SE filter spec.
sections.eli5: On the way back, one status note is attached to each road. That works unless the road branches and each branch end wants to say something different.

sections.title: Per S2L Sub-LSP Operational Status
sections.content:
To allow different egress LSRs to report different statuses, an LSR reporting the status of a P2MP S2L sub-LSP may include the LSP Attributes object in a Resv message or update one already there. Such an object MUST follow a S2L_SUB_LSP object, and only the first instance in that context is meaningful.

If an LSP Attributes object appears before the first S2L_SUB_LSP, it represents the status of all S2L sub-LSPs in the message. A branch node combining Resv state from several receivers SHOULD move that object to follow the first received S2L_SUB_LSP and duplicate it after each later one.

In the Section 3.2 BNF, the S2L sub-LSP flow descriptor is <S2L_SUB_LSP> [ <LSP_ATTRIBUTES> ... ] [ <P2MP_SECONDARY_RECORD_ROUTE> ], and LSP_ATTRIBUTES no longer appears directly in the FF flow descriptor or SE filter spec.
sections.eli5: Now each branch end of the road gets its own note, placed right after its name tag. If a general note comes first, the branching point copies it onto every branch.

sections.title: Compatibility
sections.content:
A node that supports RFC 4875 and RFC 5420 but not this document will read the first LSP Attributes object in a message formatted this way as LSP operational status, not S2L sub-LSP status.

The RFC says it is unclear whether this is a significant issue, because the LSP Attributes object is currently considered unsuitable for reporting operational status of P2MP LSPs (see Section 2.1 of RFC 6511). The intent is to correct that limitation, and networks that want such reporting are expected to deploy this extension.
sections.eli5: Older equipment will misread the new notes as being about the whole road. The authors expect only networks that want the new feature to switch on the change.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document clarifies the use of objects defined in RFC 5420. No new information is conveyed, so it adds no security considerations of its own. For general MPLS and GMPLS security issues it points to the security framework in RFC 5920.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is being said, only where to write it down, so no new safety worries arise.
